items.title: Directive (EU) 2026/470 amending Directives 2006/43/EC, 2013/34/EU, (EU) 2022/2464 and (EU) 2024/1760 (the Omnibus I Directive)
items.publisher: Publications Office of the European Union (Official Journal of the European Union)
items.locator: Recital 12; Article 2(1), (4) and (5), amending Articles 1(3), 19a and 29a of Directive 2013/34/EU; Article 3, amending Article 5(2) of Directive (EU) 2022/2464; Articles 5 and 6
items.quote: There is evidence that undertakings in the value chain, including small and medium-sized enterprises, receive disproportionate requests for information from reporting undertakings
items.why: The binding EU rule and the source of the quotation. Mandatory sustainability reporting now applies only to undertakings that exceed both EUR 450 000 000 net turnover and an average of 1 000 employees; listed small and medium-sized undertakings are removed from scope. Reporting undertakings must still report on their value chain, which is how the duty reaches suppliers. Published 26 February 2026, in force on the twentieth day after publication; member states must transpose Articles 1 to 3 by 19 March 2027. Official Journal text served by the Publications Office because EUR-Lex returned empty pages. The page prints '1 000' with a non-breaking space.

items.title: Commission Staff Working Document SWD(2026) 500 final, accompanying the two delegated regulations of 3 July 2026
items.locator: Section on the context of the ESRS revision, PDF page 4 (printed page 3); section 2.3, PDF page 10 (printed page 9); passage on the value chain cap, PDF page 6 (printed page 5)
items.quote: reducing the number of companies in scope by about 85%
items.why: Source of the figure. The Commission's own estimate of how far the 2026 directive narrowed mandatory reporting; repeated later in the document as '85 %'. Also explains that the cap uses a single employee test, so a company with more than 1 000 employees but turnover below EUR 450 million neither reports nor is protected. An estimate by the Commission's services, not a count.

items.title: Directive (EU) 2025/794 as regards the dates from which Member States are to apply certain corporate sustainability reporting and due diligence requirements (the 'stop-the-clock' Directive)
items.publisher: Publications Office of the European Union (Official Journal of the European Union)
items.locator: Article 1 (amending Article 5(2) of Directive (EU) 2022/2464); Article 3 (transposition by 31 December 2025)
items.quote: as regards the dates from which Member States are to apply certain corporate sustainability reporting and due diligence requirements
items.why: The earlier of the two changes. Moved the second and third groups of companies from financial years 2025 and 2026 to financial years starting on or after 1 January 2027 and 1 January 2028. Needed to date any customer's first report correctly; the 2026 directive then removed most of those companies from scope altogether. Official Journal text served by the Publications Office.

items.title: Corporate sustainability reporting
items.publisher: European Commission, Directorate-General for Financial Stability, Financial Services and Capital Markets Union
items.locator: Sections 'What the EU is doing and why' and 'Policy making timeline' (entries for 14 April 2025, 30 July 2025, 9 December 2025 and 3 July 2026)
items.quote: EU law requires companies above a certain size to disclose information on what they see as the risks and opportunities
items.why: The Commission's own timeline of the changes: the stop-the-clock directive, the 2025 recommendation of the voluntary standard, the political agreement on Omnibus I and the adoption of the two delegated acts on 3 July 2026. Last updated 3 July 2026, so it does not record that the delegated acts were published in the Official Journal on 21 September 2026. A horizon-scanning page, not a legal text.

items.title: PS26/19: Aligning listed issuers' sustainability disclosures with international standards
items.locator: Sections 'Who this is for' and 'Next steps'
items.quote: The new rules apply to accounting periods starting on or after 1 January 2027, with first reporting in 2028.
items.why: The UK duty most likely to reach suppliers. Listed companies in four listing categories must report against UK Sustainability Reporting Standards on a comply-or-explain basis, with transitional relief of one year for Scope 3 (value-chain) emissions and two years for wider sustainability disclosures. Published two days before this check. The older consultation address now redirects to this page.

items.title: UK Sustainability Reporting Standards
items.quote: The standards are available for voluntary use, by any entity that chooses to do so.
items.why: Status of the UK standards. UK SRS S1 and S2 were published in final form on 25 February 2026 and are voluntary unless another rule requires them. The page still says the regulator 'is currently consulting'; that consultation closed on 20 March 2026 and final rules followed on 30 September 2026. The page header names the department as 'Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade and Department for Business and Trade'.

items.title: Companies Act 2006, section 414CA: Non-financial and sustainability information statement
items.quote: the company had no more than 500 employees in that financial year
items.why: Which UK companies must publish a non-financial and sustainability information statement: traded, banking and insurance companies, companies on the Alternative Investment Market, and 'high turnover' companies (more than £500 million), in each case with more than 500 employees and not small or medium-sized. Lets a supplier work out which UK customers carry the duty. The page says the section is up to date to 2 October 2026 with one outstanding effect on a Schedule.

items.title: Streamlined Energy and Carbon Reporting (SECR) regulations: evaluation
items.publisher: Department for Energy Security and Net Zero
items.locator: Landing page, 'Details'; report reference RAF019/2425 (112 pages)
items.quote: large unquoted companies and LLPs that exceed the statutory thresholds for employees, turnover and balance sheet totals
items.why: Who must report energy and carbon in the UK: quoted companies and large unquoted companies and partnerships. The 2019 guidance still prints the old size thresholds (£36 million turnover, £18 million balance sheet); section 465 of the Companies Act 2006, read on legislation.gov.uk in this pass, now sets the medium-sized ceiling at £54 million and £27 million, with 250 employees unchanged. An independent evaluation commissioned by the department.

items.title: PPN 006: Taking account of Carbon Reduction Plans in the procurement of major government contracts
items.quote: with an estimated contract value above £5 million per year
items.why: The UK public-sector route by which emissions data is asked of suppliers. Central government bodies should require a Carbon Reduction Plan, with Scope 1, Scope 2 and a defined subset of Scope 3 emissions, from bidders for contracts above £5 million a year including VAT, where relevant and proportionate. Applies to central government, its agencies and non-departmental public bodies only. Updated 10 July 2025.

items.title: Modernising corporate reporting: consultation document
items.locator: Paragraphs 6, 149 to 150 and 154 to 158 (PDF pages 42 to 43)
items.quote: intends to hold a consultation on SECR and the Energy Savings Opportunity Scheme (ESOS) later in 2026
items.why: Shows the UK position is moving. The government proposes to remove the directors' report, exempt most medium-sized private companies from the strategic report, and consider how UK SRS should be reflected in the Companies Act; a separate consultation on energy and carbon reporting is promised. Open until 30 November 2026. Proposals, not law. The landing page names the department as 'Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade'.

items.title: Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2026/1563 amending Delegated Regulation (EU) 2023/2772 as regards the simplification of certain sustainability reporting standards
items.publisher: Publications Office of the European Union (Official Journal of the European Union)
items.locator: Annex, ESRS 1 General Requirements, chapter 5, paragraphs 62 to 66; Article 3 (entry into force and application)
items.quote: does not require information on each and every actor in the upstream and downstream value chain but only the inclusion of material information
items.why: The reporting standard an EU customer in scope will follow from financial years beginning on or after 1 January 2027. It tells the customer what it must gather from its value chain: material information only, which may come from suppliers directly or from estimates (paragraph 65), and paragraph 66 ties requests to protected undertakings to the Annex II datapoints of Regulation (EU) 2026/1560. This is the text a supplier's map of customer duties should be drawn from. Enters into force on 10 November 2026, so not yet in force on the day it was read. Official Journal text served by the Publications Office because EUR-Lex returned empty pages.

items.title: UK SRS S1: General Requirements for Disclosure of Sustainability-related Financial Information
items.locator: Appendix A, defined term 'value chain' (printed page 21, PDF page 25); paragraph 2 (PDF page 7); Appendix B, paragraph B5 (printed page 23, PDF page 27)
items.quote: The full range of interactions, resources and relationships related to a reporting entity's business model and the external environment in which it operates.
items.why: The UK general standard that listed customers will report against under the Financial Conduct Authority's rules. Its definition of the value chain is the reason a UK reporting customer looks to its suppliers: supply and distribution channels are named in paragraph B5. Voluntary unless another rule requires it; an investor-focused standard based on IFRS S1, not written for small firms. The existing list has the climate standard (S2) under a different criterion; this is the general standard.

items.title: Supervisory statement 5/25: Enhancing banks' and insurers' approaches to managing climate-related risks
items.publisher: Bank of England, Prudential Regulation Authority
items.locator: Paragraphs 4.25 to 4.31 (printed pages 17 to 18, PDF pages 19 to 20); chapter 1, 'Scope' (printed page 4); commencement at paragraph 3.1
items.quote: firms should seek to obtain this information where possible (eg during client onboarding or annual reviews)
items.why: The UK source for the finance column of the map. The prudential regulator expects banks and insurers to understand climate risk in their material client relationships and, where they lack the information, to seek it from clients at onboarding or annual review, or to use public data or proxies. This is the first UK regulator text found on why lenders ask borrowers for climate data; the earlier pass could read no lender source. Supervisory expectations addressed to banks and insurers, applied proportionately; they place no duty on the client. Commenced 3 December 2025 and replaced SS3/19.

items.title: Scope 3 Emissions in the UK Reporting Landscape: Call for Evidence Analysis Report
items.publisher: Department for Energy Security and Net Zero
items.locator: Chapter 2, 'SME Impacts', PDF page 18; introduction, PDF page 6 (184 responses)
items.quote: they possibly may be obliged to provide data to larger organisations, if they are a supplier to larger reporting firms
items.why: UK government evidence that value-chain reporting reaches firms outside its scope. In the analysis of responses to the 2023 call for evidence, concern about the cost and resource impact on small and medium-sized firms was raised 45 times. Dated May 2024 on the cover. A thematic analysis of 184 self-selected consultation responses, not a survey and not government policy; it predates the UK Sustainability Reporting Standards and the 2026 listing rules.

items.title: SMEs and Net Zero 2025: UK Net Zero Business Census report
items.locator: 'Tracking and measuring carbon emissions', page 17; summary table, page 16; Appendix I (survey sample and methodology), page 48
items.quote: Nearly 1 in 10 SMEs (9%) have been asked to report carbon footprint data by customers or when tendering in the last 12 months
items.why: A UK figure for how often requests actually arrive, which the brief lacks: 9% of smaller businesses overall, rising from 3% of those with no employees to 37% of medium-sized ones. Construction and utilities are the sectors most often asked. Based on 1,783 smaller businesses surveyed in the 2025 UK Net Zero Business Census; publication date printed as October 2025. A survey report by the government-owned development bank, not peer reviewed; it covers carbon data only, not wider sustainability requests. The bank's site refused automated reading on 2 October 2026 and answered on 5 October 2026.

items.title: Data Requests in Value Chains: The Effects of Corporate Sustainability Reporting on SMEs in The Netherlands
items.publisher: Niemann, Morssinkhof, van der Linden and de Vries, Sustainability 17(17), 8029 (MDPI); copy held in the Delft University of Technology repository
items.locator: Abstract (article page 1, PDF page 2); section 3.1 and Figure 1 (article page 5, PDF page 6)
items.quote: A key finding is that most Dutch SMEs (72%) have not yet received sustainability data requests.
items.why: Peer-reviewed evidence on how far reporting duties have reached suppliers so far. A survey of 431 Dutch small and medium-sized firms and 48 interviews in late 2024: 72% had received no request, but exposure rose sharply with size and with international value chains, and requests centred on carbon emissions and material use. Supports mapping customers by size and reach instead of assuming every customer will ask. Dutch sample, 19% response rate, fieldwork before the 2026 directive narrowed scope. Read in the university repository's copy of the final published version because the journal's own site refused automated reading.

items.title: Dear supplier, how sustainable are you? A multiple-case study analysis of a widespread tool for sustainable supply chain management
items.publisher: Fraser and co-authors, Sustainability Management Forum 28, 127-149 (Springer)
items.quote: Social desirability bias and supplier assessment fatigue were identified as issues confronting such questionnaires.
items.why: Peer-reviewed study of the supplier questionnaire, the instrument by which a customer's duty usually arrives. It finds that suppliers tire of repeated assessments and tend to give the answers they think are wanted, which is the research basis for the brief's point that a firm caught by surprise answers with guesses. A multiple-case study, so the findings are not statistically generalisable; published in 2020, before the EU and UK rules now in force. Open access on the publisher's site.

items.title: Fostering convergence in SME sustainability reporting (OECD SME and Entrepreneurship Papers)
items.locator: Section 1 (printed page 10, PDF page 11); executive summary (printed page 6, PDF page 7)
items.quote: Thus, despite technically being exempt from such reporting, SMEs are impacted by this "trickle-down" effect of reporting demands.
items.why: International comparator. The OECD finds the same pattern across jurisdictions: large companies and financial institutions pass their reporting needs to small suppliers and borrowers, in the absence of a common framework. Shows the position is not peculiar to the EU or the UK. A policy paper approved by the OECD Committee on SMEs and Entrepreneurship on 20 January 2025; it describes the EU voluntary standard while still a draft and predates the 2026 directive.
